clinicalPearls: Caused by mutations in SFTPC and usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, often with variable expression and de novo cases
Presentation ranges widely, from severe neonatal respiratory disease to childhood or adult-onset interstitial lung disease
A dominant-negative mechanism means that even a single abnormal allele can cause disease, unlike the recessive surfactant protein B deficiency
Imaging typically shows diffuse interstitial change, ground-glass opacity and, over time, cysts or fibrosis
The clinical course is highly variable within and between families carrying the same mutation
Diagnosis combines genetic testing with imaging and, where needed, lung biopsy
Management is supportive, sometimes with immunomodulatory therapy, and lung transplantation for advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Surfactant protein C is a hydrophobic protein that contributes to surfactant function and is produced by alveolar type II cells. Many SFTPC mutations lead to misfolding of the proprotein, which accumulates within type II cells and triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, cellular injury and an abnormal repair response. This cellular toxicity, rather than simple loss of protein, drives progressive interstitial inflammation and fibrosis. The dominant-negative and gain-of-toxicity effects explain the autosomal dominant inheritance and the wide variability in age of onset and severity.
additionalDifferentials: Other childhood interstitial lung disease (chILD) entities
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Lung biopsy when the diagnosis is unclear
Pulmonary function testing in older children and adults
Family screening and assessment given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Rapidly progressive respiratory failure at any age
Progressive fibrosis with declining lung function
Superimposed respiratory infection causing acute deterioration
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is variable, ranging from severe fatal neonatal disease to a chronic course into adulthood; some patients stabilise while others progress to fibrosis requiring transplantation.
pitfalls: Assuming an adult with interstitial lung disease cannot have a genetic surfactant disorder
Expecting a uniform course from a given mutation
Missing the diagnosis in a family labelled as having idiopathic fibrosis
Overlooking the need to screen relatives for dominant inheritance
references: Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children (standard reference)
management: Trial empirical anti-inflammatory therapy with systemic corticosteroids, sometimes combined with hydroxychloroquine, to modify the interstitial inflammation, though evidence is limited
Provide supplemental oxygen and other supportive care for chronic interstitial lung disease
Ensure routine, influenza and pneumococcal immunisation and treat respiratory infections promptly to limit exacerbations
Reserve lung transplantation for progressive end-stage fibrotic disease
Monitor disease with serial pulmonary function testing and high-resolution CT
Manage care through a paediatric or adult interstitial lung disease multidisciplinary team
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance with de novo cases and variable expression
